A multi-specialty hospital I worked with in the UAE was getting plenty of leads from its Meta ads. Cheap ones, too. The problem? Very few turned into booked appointments. So here's how to run social media ads that actually work: decide the business result first, track that result properly, pick one objective, keep the structure simple, give the platform three to five creatives, then leave it alone for a week. Judge it on bookings or sales, not on what the ad platform reports.
That's the short answer. Here's the story behind it, and the seven decisions I now make before any Meta or TikTok campaign goes live.
Paid social ads create demand by reaching people who aren't searching yet, so the offer and the creative do more of the work than tight targeting does.
On Meta, Advantage+ audience is switched on by default for Leads, Sales and App campaigns, so your real levers are the objective, the conversion signal and the creative.
Track the result you care about with the Meta Pixel and Conversions API, or the TikTok Pixel and Events API, and optimise for that event, not an early click.
Meta says an ad set usually needs about 50 optimisation events in a week to leave the learning phase, so budget for that and avoid big edits for the first seven days.
Judge campaigns in your CRM. Reported conversions can rise without real customers rising, especially since Meta started measuring some conversions on customers' devices in November 2026.

What are paid social ads, in plain language?
Paid social ads are posts you pay a platform such as Facebook, Instagram or TikTok to show to people who don't follow you. They appear in the feed, Stories or Reels, marked "Sponsored".
You can run them in two ways. You can press "Boost" on a post you've already published, or you can build a campaign in Meta Ads Manager or TikTok Ads Manager.
Boosting is quick, but it gives you very few choices. Ads Manager lets you choose the objective, the conversion you want, the lead form, the budget and the creative.
If the goal is leads or sales, use Ads Manager. Boost is for reach, not results.
Paid social creates demand. Search catches it.
Most of my work sits in search and Performance Max. So I came to paid social with a search marketer's habits, and some of them were wrong.
On Google, the person is already looking. They've typed "cardiologist near me". On Meta or TikTok, they're scrolling past a friend's holiday photos. Your ad interrupts them.
That changes what does the work.
The person is looking for you
The person is scrolling past you
You catch demand that already exists
You create demand that didn't exist a second ago

A click is a weak signal, so optimise for the real result

Why the hospital's cheap leads cost it more

Back to the hospital. Last year, its Meta campaigns looked healthy in Ads Manager. Leads were coming in, and they were cheap. The call centre told a different story. Many people didn't pick up. Some didn't remember filling in a form.
So I went through the account. Three things stood out.
The forms let anyone through. They were instant forms on Meta's default "More volume" type, with no questions beyond name and number. One tap and the lead was sent.
The budget was sliced too thin. It was spread across many ad sets, each with its own narrow interest audience. None of them got enough results to learn.
The campaign was learning from the wrong thing. It ran on an Engagement objective, so Meta optimised for taps and interactions, not submitted leads. So Meta found people who tap, not people who book.

Here's what I changed. I switched the forms to the "Higher intent" type, which adds a review screen before the lead is sent, and added two qualifying questions: which speciality they needed, and when they'd like to come in. I merged the ad sets into a few broad ones. I moved it to the Leads objective and optimised for the submitted lead. And I added more creative variations, in Arabic and English.
The result? Cost per lead came down, and far more of those leads became booked appointments.
Cheap leads are only cheap until someone has to call them.

This is what I fill in before any campaign goes live. Each line is a decision, not a setting. If you can't answer one, you're not ready to launch.
Goal. The business result you'll judge it on, such as a booked appointment or a sale. Not a platform metric.
Platform. Where your customers actually scroll. Start with one.
Signal. The event you'll optimise for, tracked in the browser and from your server.
Objective. One campaign objective that matches the signal, such as Leads or Sales.
Structure. As few ad sets as you can, with broad audiences.
Creative. Three to five variations, made for the feed, in every language your customers use.
Patience. A budget that can buy about 50 results a week, and seven days without big edits.
Notice what isn't on the list: interests. On Meta today, they're mostly a suggestion.
How to run social media ads: your first campaign, step by step
Here's the order I follow on Meta. TikTok Ads Manager follows a similar path.
Set up your accounts. Create a business portfolio in Meta Business Suite and an ad account inside it. On TikTok, create a TikTok for Business account and an ad account.

Install tracking. Add the Meta Pixel to your site and connect the Conversions API, which sends events from your server as well as the browser. On TikTok, use the Pixel and the Events API together, with event deduplication switched on. Test the events before you spend anything.
Choose the objective. Pick Leads or Sales, whichever matches decision 1. Avoid Traffic or Engagement if what you want is customers.
Set the budget and schedule. Start with one campaign and a budget that can realistically buy about 50 results a week. Plan to run it for at least seven days.
Set the audience. Add location, language and a minimum age. Leave Advantage+ audience on, and add a customer list as a suggestion if you have one.
Leave placements on automatic, unless you have a clear reason not to.

Build the form or landing page. For instant forms, choose "Higher intent" and add one or two qualifying questions. For a website, make sure the page loads fast on a phone and fires the conversion event.
Add three to five creatives. Vertical video, captions on, and the hook in the first second or two. Make Arabic and English versions if your audience uses both.
Check the creative settings, then publish. More on that in the Bonus Tip below.
How much should you spend, and how long should you wait?

Both platforms need data before delivery settles. Meta calls this the learning phase. Its help centre says an ad set usually leaves it after about 50 optimisation events in the week after its last significant edit.
TikTok's help page, updated June 2026, says volatility usually starts to fall after about 25 results or seven days. Its FAQ calls 50 conversions the strongest sign that the phase is over.

That gives you a simple budget check. Take your expected cost per result and multiply it by 50. That's roughly what one ad set needs in a week. TikTok's own advice is close: a budget about 50 times your target cost per action.
Weekly budget per ad set: AED 80 × 50 = AED 4,000
Illustrative example. Use your own cost per result.
If you can't afford that, don't split the money further. Use fewer ad sets, or optimise for an event that happens more often.
Then wait. Pausing, big budget jumps and new creative can all restart learning, on both platforms.
Give it a week. It's the one thing I'd tell a friend running their first ad tomorrow.
How do you tell if paid social is actually working?
The ad platform will tell you it's working. That's its job. Your job is to check.
Tag every ad link with UTM parameters, so GA4 and your CRM can see which campaign each lead came from. My free UTM builder does this in a few seconds.
Compare the platform's lead count with what your CRM or call centre records. Look at cost per booked appointment or sale, not cost per lead.
Send the outcome back where you can. Meta's Conversions API can carry offline and CRM events, such as a qualified lead.

Watch for reporting changes. From 12 November 2026, the Meta Pixel started measuring some conversions on the customer's device, switched on by default outside the EU and UK. As Stape points out, more attributed conversions doesn't necessarily mean more real ones.
If the platform says things got better and the CRM says nothing changed, believe the CRM.
Paid social isn't the answer to everything. Here's where I've seen it struggle.
Small budgets. If an ad set can't reach about 50 results a week, it often shows "Learning limited" in Ads Manager. You can optimise for a more frequent event, but that's a weaker signal.
Long or offline sales cycles. If the real result happens weeks later on a phone call, the platform learns from the form, not the customer. Feed CRM outcomes back, or accept the lag.
Regulated categories. Healthcare ads in the UAE have to follow the health authorities' advertising rules. I covered some of this in my post on digital marketing for doctors.

Less control. With Advantage+ audience on, Meta treats most of your targeting as a suggestion. Some practitioners still prefer tighter control for niche B2B or very local audiences, and that's a fair view. Test it rather than assume.
Bonus Tip: check what Meta's AI is allowed to change

Before you publish, open each ad's creative settings and review the Advantage+ creative enhancements. Meta's help page says some enhancements may be on by default. In healthcare, an automatic text tweak can turn a careful line into a claim you're not allowed to make. Turn off anything you wouldn't sign off yourself.
Open Events Manager and confirm you're tracking the real result, not a click.
Count your ad sets. If the budget can't buy about 50 results a week for each, merge them.
Switch lead forms to "Higher intent" and add one or two qualifying questions.
Add three to five creatives, in every language your customers use.
Write down today's date, and don't touch anything for seven days.
How much do paid social ads cost?

There's no fixed price, because you bid in an auction and costs change by market, audience and season. A useful starting budget is one that can buy about 50 of your chosen results in a week. If a lead costs AED 80, that's around AED 4,000 a week for one ad set. TikTok suggests a budget about 50 times your target cost per action.
Is boosting a post the same as running an ad?

Not quite. Boosting promotes a post you've already published, with a few simple targeting and budget choices. Running an ad in Meta Ads Manager or TikTok Ads Manager lets you choose the objective, the conversion event, the lead form and several creatives. If you want leads or sales, Ads Manager gives you far more control over what you're paying for.
How long do paid social ads take to work?

Plan for at least seven days before judging a new campaign. Meta says an ad set usually leaves the learning phase after about 50 optimisation events in a week. TikTok says volatility usually falls after about 25 results or seven days. Results during learning are often unstable, so avoid pausing or making big edits in that first week.
Should I run Meta ads or Google Ads?

They do different jobs, so many businesses run both. Google Ads catches people who are already searching for what you offer. Meta and TikTok reach people who aren't searching yet, which creates new demand. If your budget is small and people already search for your service, start with search, then add paid social to grow demand.
Do I need the Meta Pixel to run social ads?

You can run instant-form lead ads without a website pixel, but you need tracking to optimise for anything that happens on your site. Meta recommends pairing the Pixel with the Conversions API. On TikTok, a Pixel or Events API setup is required for its website conversions objective. Either way, test your events before you spend.
